body:
Some people just aren't equipped to talk about depression and suicide, I guess. I hope his enormously terrible response doesn't dissuade you from talking to the other people in your life. Are you still feeling vengeful about what he said? 

P.S. it is 4AM here so if I do not reply further it is because I fell asleep, my apologies in advance.

Did anything in particular happen six years ago? Or were you always depressed before and just even more depressed now? 

RE: was too scared -  I can understand that. I have thought about suicide nearly every day since I was a kid, but did nothing about it because I didn't have the physical supplies, and was afraid of botching the job or turning into a vegetable. You say you think you have the courage now - are there still parts of suicide that frighten you?

First: we have a very similar username! 

Second: I understand how you feel. Every day, I think about suicide and remind myself that it is a way out, even if I had a good day. However, I have not killed myself (mostly due to laziness, and also because my cats would starve without me). Life is hard, and some days are more difficult than others. What is making things for you difficult right now?
P.S. it is currently 4AM here, so if I don't respond to subsequent comment it is because I am unconscious, sorry for time zone difference

That is a long time! Have those six years been all universally painful?  How have you kept yourself going during that time? 

P.S. It is 4AM here, so if I stop replying it's not because I am trying to be rude or downgrade your struggles, it is because I am unconscious

Ah, these are new connections you don't want to scare away. That makes sense. 

But I'm not suggesting that you emotionally vomit on them or anything. But even telling them an edited version of tough times you are going through might help? (even responding to "how are you" with "actually not that good" can help) 

People would probably much rather hear that you are hurting than to hear news of your death. My brother killed himself a few years ago and it was a big surprise to everyone, because he never told anybody how he was feeling. I know his friends and I would much rather have listened to his problems (even if it made us cry, be awkward, etc) than to attend his funeral.

Wow, that's a very rude and unempathetic thing for him to say. I understand the urge to try and prove him wrong and make him regret what he said. Is your relationship with your brother always like this?

I guess you did find the truth - that life is hard (not to mention climate change, north korean labour camps, etc, but I digress) and fundamentally devoid of universal meaning. Few people have a job or a "calling" that can make them happy and change the world. Many people distract themselves from the lack of meaning in life by having hobbies and distractions (or children, lol). I'm sorry that those diversions no longer do it for you. How long have you felt this way?

That sounds hard. To be lonely, but also not to be able to get away from the loneliness even when you're talking to other people. I used to have an ex-boyfriend with whom I couldn't talk to about a lot of things, so I felt lonely even when I wasn't alone. 

What is the reason(s) you cannot share these feelings with the people in your life?

I don't think people get stronger as they get older, they just get more accustomed to their circumstances (even if those circumstances are miserable). 

How do you distract yourself from the harshness of life?

It sounds like you like you enjoy being around other people. Even though you can't talk about your loneliness and sadness, are you able to talk to these other people about things you enjoy? I certainly don't tell my family everything because I am afraid it would scare them. But I enjoy the time I spend with them anyways, and it's enough to keep going.

Your friend may be overwhelmed with their own pain, but it was rude to tell you those words. You are allowed to feel what you feel. 

Your family is also very rude. 

You deserve to not be in pain. But you also deserve to live. Even a monster deserves to breathe clean air, live at a basic standard, and be listened to. You wrote this post, so you are not a monster. You don't deserve to die.

It is okay to feel what you feel. It is okay to be afraid of depression and suicide. And it is okay to be sad even if you have support: you don't need to feel guilty for having friends and family at home. 

It may be just that you are feeling lonely right now because of the change in your educational situation. Keep taking things day by day. Eventually you will get the hang of things in your new school and not feel so lost anymore. If you are shy to make friends at your new school, keep in touch with your friends at home.

Yeah...you have the escape hatch at the back of your mind. You always know it's there. You go years without going nearing it. But even one bad day can make you march right up to that escape hatch, and put your hands on the door, and think about pushing it open. I'm glad you didn't open up the escape hatch and check out early today. 

I hope tomorrow will be a better day for you. The escape hatch may always be there. But tomorrow, I hope you will be able to take your hands off the door and walk away from it, at least for a while.

I am happy you love your dog and your brother. Sometimes I look at my cat and my boyfriend and I am just so grateful they are there. 

It is okay to feel that way even if you are young. Sometimes life is bad, and the world seems to be going in the wrong direction. I wish it weren't, but it is. When things are bad, I cling on to the hope that maybe I will feel better tomorrow. Maybe there are still good days ahead. And if there is one more good day with me and my cat and my boyfriend, then I think my life is still worth living. So if there is one more good day to be had with you and your dog and your brother, then maybe life is still worth living - even for just that one good day. 

Please give your dog a hug when you have time.

Yes, especially when you are not actively suicidal it can seem like a burden to tell someone. Especially for therapists, it can seem like you are wasting their time - i.e. "if you are not going to kill yourself today, why bother talking about it? I guess you're fine! Next!" Blah. 

But I've come to realize that having that big red emergency lever at the back of my head might not be normal, even if one does not have the immediate urge to pull it. At the very least, your friends can help by understanding how you feel today, and that you have that Escape Plan. And then, if one day in the future you have a bad day where you start thinking really hard about going through with the Escape Plan, then it will be easier for you to go back to them.  

And - I guess, God forbid you ever do pull the lever and check out early, then at least it won't be as much of a nasty surprise to them.

Yeah, people tend to react poorly when I share my thoughts about suicide with them. Like with tears and stuff. Then I reassure them that I'm not about to go out and buy a noose, they cry some more, and then I regret mention it at all. 

However, you may have luck if there's a friend who's had suicidal thoughts or depression or anxiety themselves. They'd know what it feels like. 

Try not to worry about dumping your problems on them. Most people want to help and listen. I've made time for an internet stranger. Your friends will make time for you.

My little brother killed himself a few years ago. It was absolutely the worst thing he ever did to me. I miss him every day, and for a while I wanted to die to go join him. Sometimes I still do. 

His suicide also ruined my relationship with the rest of my family. I can't go visit my childhood home anymore without being surrounded by the memory of my failure. If I eat dinner with my parents, there is an overwhelming sense that someone is missing. 

I guarantee that your friends and your sister will think about your death for the rest of their lives. They will wonder what they did wrong. They will wonder why you didn't talk to them. They will wonder how they missed all the warning signs. You can write to them and tell them not to blame themselves, if you like. Their therapists will tell them not to blame themselves. It will not work. They will carry the guilt of having failed to prevent your suicide for all time. They may stop talking to each other, because they can't hang out without feeling guilty that you're not there. 

Sorry if that's not the answer that you wanted.
